en: Points of Controversy The Great Fifty-Section The Fourteenth Chapter
Discussion on the Condition of Immediate Succession:
Is it the case that ear-consciousness arises immediately after eye-consciousness? Yes.

Is that which is the turning toward, ... down to ... the aspiration for the arising of eye-consciousness, the same as the turning toward, ... down to ... the aspiration for the arising of ear-consciousness?
You should not say so ... [and so on] ...
Eye-consciousness arises immediately after [the cessation of] eye-consciousness; it should not be said—

“Is that which is the turning toward, ... [and so on] ... the aspiration for the arising of eye-consciousness, the very same as the turning toward, ... [and so on] ... the aspiration for the arising of ear-consciousness?”—Yes.
Does ear-consciousness arise for one who does not turn toward it, ... [and so on] ... for one who does not aspire for it?
It should not be said so … [as before] … Is it not the case that ear-consciousness arises for one who is turning [the mind], … [as before] … for one who is directing [the mind]?
Yes, it is.
If ear-consciousness arises for one who is turning [the mind] toward it …pe… for one who is directing [the mind] toward it, then surely you should not say:
“Ear-consciousness arises immediately after eye-consciousness.
Does ear-consciousness arise immediately after eye-consciousness?
“Yes.
“Does eye-consciousness arise for one who attends to the sign of form?
“Yes.”
Does auditory consciousness arise for one who attends to the sign of a visible form?
One should not say so...
[and so on] ...Is visual consciousness indeed only that which has a visible form as its object, and not something else as its object?
“Yes.
[The opponent asks: “Is auditory consciousness only that which has visible form as its object, and not that which has any other object? [The respondent replies:
“One should not say so,” and so forth.
Is it the case that eye-consciousness arises dependent upon the eye and forms?
Yes. Is it the case that ear-consciousness arises dependent upon the eye and forms?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Does ear-consciousness arise in dependence on the eye and visible forms? Yes.
“Dependent on the eye and forms, ear-consciousness arises”—
is there such a sutta? No,
there is not.
“Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises”—
is there such a sutta? Yes.
If it is true that “eye-consciousness arises dependent on the eye and forms”—
as this sutta passage indeed exists— then surely, sir, you should not say:
“ear-consciousness arises dependent on the ear and sounds.”
Is it the case that ear-consciousness arises immediately after eye-consciousness?
Yes. Is that very same eye-consciousness the ear-consciousness? No.
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Immediately after auditory consciousness,
olfactory consciousness arises … [as before] … Immediately after olfactory consciousness, gustatory consciousness arises … [as before] …
Is it the case that body-consciousness arises immediately after tongue-consciousness? Yes.

Is the turning toward [the object], the inclination, and the aspiration for the arising of tongue-consciousness the same as the turning toward, the inclination, and the aspiration for the arising of body-consciousness? [No.]
If you do not say this … [as before] … bodily consciousness arises immediately after tongue-consciousness, should it not be said:

“That turning toward, … [and so on] … that aspiration which leads to the arising of tongue-consciousness is the same as the turning toward, … [and so on] … that aspiration which leads to the arising of bodily consciousness”?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Does body-consciousness arise for one who does not turn [the mind] toward it …pe… for one who does not direct [the intention] toward it?
You should not speak thus …pe…
But is it not the case that body-consciousness arises for one who turns [the mind] toward it … pe … and arises for one who directs [it] toward it?
Yes.
If body-consciousness arises for one who turns [the mind] toward it … pe … and arises for one who directs [it] toward it, then indeed, you should not say: [that it does not arise].
“Body-consciousness arises immediately after tongue-consciousness.
Does body-consciousness arise immediately after tongue-consciousness? Yes.
Is tongue-consciousness produced for one who attends to the sign of taste?
Yes. Is body-consciousness produced for one who attends to the sign of taste?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Is tongue-consciousness an object of taste alone and not of any other object? Yes.
Is body-consciousness only objectified by taste and not by any other object?
You should not say so… [as before] … Does tongue-consciousness arise in dependence upon both the tongue and tastes?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Then is it the case that body-consciousness arises in dependence on the tongue and tastes?
You should not say so … [and so forth] … .
“Dependent on the tongue and dependent on tastes, body-consciousness arises”?—
Yes. “Dependent on the tongue and dependent on tastes, body-consciousness arises”— [this is so].
Is there indeed such a sutta? No, there is not.
[It says:
“Dependent on the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness arises.”
Is this indeed a sutta?
Yes. If it is so, then:
"Dependent upon the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness arises."
If that sutta is indeed so, then surely you must not say:
"Dependent on the tongue and tastes, body-consciousness arises.
Does body-consciousness arise immediately after tongue-consciousness?
“Yes.
“Then is that very same tongue-consciousness also body-consciousness?
“One should not say so,” and so forth.
Is it not to be said that the five types of consciousness arise as immediate antecedents to one another?
Yes, they are.
Is it not the case that there is someone who dances, sings, or plays music, and who sees a form, hears a sound, smells an odor, tastes a flavor, and touches a tangible object?
Yes, that is so.
If indeed there is someone who dances, sings, or plays music, and who sees a form, hears a sound, smells an odor, tastes a flavor, and touches a tangible object, then, surely, you must say this:
“The five types of consciousness arise in immediate succession to one another.
The discussion on the condition of contiguity is finished.
